stories.headline: Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
stories.deck: Targeting the entire organisation directly could ​severely undermine the court's work; ICC officials warn courtwide sanctions could disrupt IT, insurance, investigators and ‌payments to U.S. employees
stories.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said, a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it. U.S. officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered as one of the options.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sanctions against the court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear. The Wall Street Journal cited officials who said the decision could be finalised as soon as this week during the United Nations General Assembly meeting.
Targeting the entire organisation directly, as well as entities that cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court’s work.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the U.S. Treasury would prohibit U.S. citizens and companies from providing funds, goods, or services to the court without a license from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Banks often over-comply with such U.S. sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organisation are the purchasing of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC’s registrar and president have warned.
Mr. Trump’s opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalise ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Mr. Trump was reelected and the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.
The United States has never been a member.
Published - September 21, 2026 07:11 am IST

stories.headline: Iran rules out reopening Strait of Hormuz, returning to US talks until conditions met
stories.deck: Iran remains steadfast in its decision to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed and discontinue negotiations until its stipulations are satisfied. Tehran has communicated its demands to Washington via third parties, now awaiting a response. The nation has issued a warning regarding potential attacks on US bases should military action ensue, while US forces have redirected commercial vessels amidst a…
stories.bodyText:
Iran has ruled out reopening the Strait of Hormuz or returning to the previous framework of negotiations with the United States until Washington meets Tehran’s conditions, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said, as tensions between the two countries continue to escalate.
According to Iran’s Tasnim news agency, Ghalibaf said Tehran had conveyed its demands to Washington through intermediaries and would not change its position until its conditions were met.
“Until these conditions are met, the legitimate rights of the Iranian nation are recognised, and the Americans’ commitments are implemented, there will be no opening for a return to the previous conditions for negotiations or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
The remarks came a day after Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran had conveyed its conditions for ending the conflict to Washington through Qatar.
“Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade,” Rezaei told Al Jazeera.
The Strait of Hormuz has become a key point of contention in the confrontation. Iran’s Armed Forces spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi said the initiative in the strategic waterway remained with Iran’s armed forces, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency. 
He also rejected US statements on maritime traffic through the strait as a psychological operation.
Iran has also issued fresh warnings over possible US military action. The Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters said any renewed US attack would trigger attacks against American bases and interests across the region, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
“Should the United States make any mistake against the Islamic Republic of Iran, all its bases and interests in the region will be targeted in continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitation or consideration,” the military command said.
The Iranian command also warned regional countries against supporting any US military operation against Tehran, saying countries that assist Washington would be considered participants in the action, according to IRNA.
Meanwhile, US central command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels as part of efforts to enforce Washington’s naval blockade against Iran. CENTCOM said the vessels were redirected as of September 20 to ensure compliance with the blockade.
The US military resumed enforcement of the naval blockade against maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports on July 14, according to CENTCOM.
US President Donald Trump has meanwhile warned Iran of consequences if Tehran refuses to change its position, while also indicating that he could be open to talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The latest developments come as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly, with the US-Iran confrontation and wider West Asia tensions expected to remain major issues during the diplomatic gathering.

stories.headline: Russia reports mass cyberattacks targeting elections
stories.deck: The chair of Russia’s Central Election Commission said the attacks appeared to have been carried out by “highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools”
stories.bodyText:
Russia’s electoral chief said Sunday (September 20, 2026) that there had been over 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks targeting Russian election infrastructure in recent days.
Ella Pamfilova, chair of Russia’s Central Election Commission, did not say who was responsible.
The attacks appeared to have been carried out by “highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools,” she said.
DDoS attacks involve overwhelming a system with internet traffic so that it is unable to function normally.
“Over the past period, more than 1,000 waves of DDoS attacks have been recorded against infrastructure in Russia that is specifically involved in the electoral process,” Ms. Pamfilova was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies.
Voting is currently under way in Russia to determine all 450 seats in the lower house, the State Duma.
The ruling United Russia party, which backs President Vladimir Putin and has won every parliamentary election in Russia since 2003, is widely expected to secure another victory.
All other parties cleared to run back Mr. Putin and the Ukraine offensive, while Russia’s Supreme Court struck the anti-war Yabloko party off the ballot weeks before the vote.

stories.headline: Australia wants a seat at the UN table from 2029. Can it get one?
stories.bodyText: Australia will bid to join the United Nations Security Council from 2029, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Monday, as he launched a campaign to secure one of the two non-permanent seats available to its bloc.Albanese said Australia, whose last two-year term on the council ended in 2014, would have an opportunity to play a key role in shaping global responses to issues that matter to Australians if elected to the Security Council."Australia punches above our weight ... and we can have an impact on the world, and that's what I want to see Australia do," Albanese told reporters in New York on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders at the UN General Assembly.Albanese said he expected "very strong support" from Pacific island countries and Southeast Asia.He added that his "strong relationships" with world leaders would help Australia's bid, even as a closely watched Newspoll conducted for The Australian newspaper and released on Monday showed his approval rating at home had slipped to its lowest level since he won its first term in 2022..'Navigational rights must not be subject to coercion, threats': India tells UNSC.Rapid developments in AI and the effects of climate change will be among the world's top challenges by the end of this decade, making it in Australia's national interest to be involved in the UN Security Council, Albanese said.The UN Security Council has 10 non-permanent members, with five elected each year. Finland is the other nominee, alongside Australia, for the 2029-30 seat from the Western European and Others Group. The Asia-Pacific, African, and Latin American and Caribbean groups will also put forward their nominees.Voting to select the non-permanent members for the 2029-2030 term is expected to take place by secret ballot in 2028.The United States, China, France, Russia, and the United Kingdom make up the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

briefs.headline: Early returns in Russia’s parliamentary election show main Kremlin party leading
briefs.deck: With some 58% of the precincts counted, United Russia had nearly 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies apportioned by party lists, according to the Central Election Commission
briefs.bodyText:
Early results from Russia's first wartime parliamentary election, released by the country's election commission early Monday (September 21, 2026), showed the main Kremlin party dominating the vote.
The tightly controlled balloting was virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.
With some 58% of the precincts counted, United Russia had nearly 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies apportioned by party lists, according to the Central Election Commission.
Another 225 lawmakers will be chosen in single-seat races, and United Russia also was poised to win most of those.
The balloting included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began, but still doesn't fully control, as well as those in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, in what Kyiv denounced as illegal and the European Union described as a “blatant violation of international law”.
Success in the polls by United Russia, backed by President Vladimir Putin, will help the Kremlin keep its tight grip on power.
The vote, which saw most opposition barred from running, took place against the backdrop of the harshest political crackdowns and freedom of speech in Russia since Soviet times.
The early results showed that four other parties almost always vote for Kremlin initiatives returning to the State Duma, the lower chamber of parliament.

briefs.headline: Russian election, cast as test of support for Ukraine war, enters final day
briefs.deck: Most anti-war candidates ‌were barred from the ballot; those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities
briefs.bodyText:
A parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia’s war in Ukraine entered its third and final day on Sunday (September 20, 2026), with the ruling United Russia party expected to retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is likely to be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public backing for Mr. Putin’s policies and for the war, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities.
Also Read: Early returns in Russia’s parliamentary election show main Kremlin party leading
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
Permitted opposition parties could benifit
Mr. Putin on Friday (September 18, 2026) accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that killed Elena Astanina, the official. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no immediate comment from Kyiv.
Russian electoral officials also said on Saturday (September 19, 2026) that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election”.
Despite what most experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated “a foreign agent”, said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues.
Mr. Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
“Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” said Mr. Putin.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 1800 GMT on Sunday (September 20, 2026), with more complete results available on Monday (September 21, 2026).

briefs.headline: 'I won't leave it until I win': Khan returns for his 4th Asiad with same Oly dream
briefs.deck: As Mairaj Ahmad Khan prepares for his fourth Asian Games, the Olympic gold that has stayed out of reach for more than two decades remains his biggest motivation. From cricket fields in Bulandshahr to becoming India's first Olympic skeet shooter and the country's first men's skeet World Cup champion, the 50-year-old reflects on Rio, COVID, personal loss, Cairo, and the philosophy that continues to…
briefs.bodyText:
As Mairaj Ahmad Khan prepares for his fourth Asian Games, the medal occupying most of his thoughts isn't the one on offer in Japan.
It is the one that has stayed out of reach for more than two decades.
"Olympic gold, which I haven't got yet. The fight is for that. I won't leave it until I win. My first dream was to become an Olympian. That dream came true. Now the dream is to become an Olympic champion."
At 50, Mairaj has already rewritten parts of Indian skeet shooting history. He became the first Indian skeet shooter to qualify for the Olympic Games, later became the first Indian to win a men's skeet World Cup gold, and has represented the country at two Olympics.
Mairaj’s first Asian Games came in Doha in 2006, and after missing selection in Jakarta 2018 and Hangzhou 2022, he now returns to the Indian team nearly two decades after his Asian Games debut. The men's skeet qualification begins on September 21, with the final scheduled for September 23.
Away from the range, he has little interest in turning himself into something larger than he is.
"Miraj Ahmed Khan is a very normal person. I live my life like a normal person. 
If I don't shoot, I don't think about shooting. I don't keep talking about shooting all the time. I'm still working to tell everyone Miraj Ahmed Khan is alive and rocking."
Before skeet, there was cricket
Long before skeet shooting became his profession, cricket had his attention. "Mera pehla pyaar cricket tha. Main cricket hi khelta tha. Shooting toh ghar mein thi kyunki papa shoot karte the, lekin main cricket ke peeche tha [My first love was cricket. That's all I played. Shooting was always around at home because my father was a shooter, but my heart was set on cricket]."
Mairaj grew up in a family of zamindars where firearms were a familiar sight. His father, Late Ilyas Ahmed Khan, competed in trap shooting, and as a youngster Mairaj also tried his hand at air rifle and .22 rifle events. At a district-level three-position competition in Bulandshahr, he won ₹30 in prize money.
"I bought a cricket bat with that money," he said, laughing.
There were afternoons spent on cricket fields, also a match alongside a young Virender Sehwag and, like many teenagers, the belief that the game would continue to shape his future. Shooting remained close, but not as a career.
"Us waqt shooting ko career ki tarah koi dekhta bhi nahi tha. Main bhi nahi dekhta tha [Back then, nobody really looked at shooting as a career. I didn't either]."
Competitive shooting for Mairaj arrived later than it does for most elite athletes today. While he entered the sport in 1998, he made his international debut in 2003. By then, many of the shooters he would eventually compete against had already spent years on international ranges.
But that never troubled him. "Nobody told me that it's late now. Because at that time, shooting was not very popular in our country, especially shotgun shooting. It was an expensive sport. Only rich people used to shoot - Maharajas and businessmen."
The sport demanded far more than talent. Ammunition, travel, and equipment all came at a price. Staying in it required help.
"I was lucky. I found Mr Naveen Jindal at that time. He got me the sponsorship. And if you see, Jindal is still on my jacket. He found me and pushed me, saying, 'You can do this.'"
'Empty your cup'
That backing kept him in the sport. The belief that he could stand alongside the world's best came later; in 2013, when Atlanta Olympic champion Ennio Falco took charge as India's skeet coach.
"Before that, we were just shooting. The mindset was not a winning mentality. The mindset was just go and participate and come back. Being a tourist. Okay, we are going to Germany, we are going to Italy, we are going to South America, USA. Just like a tourist, we were travelling on government expense."
By the time Olympic champion Falco joined, Mairaj had already spent a decade on the international circuit. Falco didn't ask the shooters to change overnight. He first wanted them to change the way they thought about competition.
"You have to empty your cup."
It puzzled Mairaj at first. "At that time I didn't get it. But after a few months, I understood what he tried to tell me - that I had to empty my cup and refill it."
Two years later, he secured India's first Olympic quota in men's skeet. "I reached the Olympic Games in 2015. I won the quota place. Basically, we set our result from this practice."
Remembering Rio
Rio 2016 followed, and he still remembers it target by target. "In Rio, I was very relaxed. If you ask me frankly, and I'm telling you now, it's been 10 years, I still remember the competition as it happened yesterday only."
"Whenever I close my eyes, I can see myself on that range. I can feel the station still. I will tell you where the low house is and what colour the low house is. Its memory is still like yesterday."
Mairaj finished ninth after a shoot-off, one place outside the final. His near miss in Rio also came against the backdrop of a discipline where India has rarely found individual success at the Asian Games. Before Nagoya, only two Indians had reached the skeet podium - Karni Singh, who won bronze in Tehran in 1974, and Anant Jeet Singh Naruka, who claimed silver in Hangzhou in 2023.
"What I realised in the end was that the Olympic Games is just a competition. We basically see that competition differently. But it's the same competition of 125 targets."
For Mairaj, nothing should change simply because the Olympic rings are on the range.
"If you want to see that competition like a normal competition, like a 125-target selection trial or a World Cup or Asian Championship or Asian Games, it must be that way. It's not like the Olympic Games."
He laughed while listing the promises athletes make to themselves before the Games.
"Now I have to work. I have to run. I have to eat only diet food. I have to reduce 20 kilos from my body... No, no, no."
"The gun should be the same. Ammunition is the same. You work the same. Same way like you are preparing for a selection trial. Because you are preparing well for the selection also. If you are not selected in the Indian team, how are you going to win a quota place for the country?"
"It should be in the same flow from day one when you win the quota place till the match. In the same flow."
The years that stood still
Tokyo arrived under very different circumstances. By the time Mairaj secured another Olympic quota in Doha, he felt he was shooting as well as he ever had.
"I was in very supreme form when I won the quota place in Doha. And then immediately we had the national championship here in Delhi. I shot 125 out of 125. I was peaking at the right time."
Then the pandemic pushed the Olympics back by a year. "COVID came. And the Olympic Games moved to the next year, in 2021. You cannot carry your peak for two years."
The ranges shut. "No shooting. Every range was closed. You were inside your home. No physical fitness. Nothing."
A few months before the Games, his father died. "For me, I lost my father in April before the Olympic Games. So, it's another setback for me."
"For everyone, not just for me, the entire world was suffering with the COVID virus. Everybody was losing somebody - family, relations."
"We were in Italy. It was like zombie land. We were training on the shooting range alone. Because when you are shooting alone, it's not that feeling. You need somebody to shoot with you. How will you compete when you go there, and there are six shooters in the squad, and you are training all alone?"
And that interruption lingered well beyond Tokyo as well for Mairaj. "That was very difficult for me, and I didn't overcome it, and I didn't win the Paris quota place. That journey was very, very difficult."
"From 2020... till now, I'm struggling. I started peaking now, slowly, slowly. I won a competition, a small competition. I won the selection. I won a medal in the national championship."
"I've changed the gun now. I've changed the technique to catch something. But it takes time. In skeet, if you change one bit, you go behind 10 bits."
The comeback that began in Cairo
But even in the middle of his struggles, there was a sliver of hope in the form of World Cup gold in 2022 in Cairo, Egypt.
The gold was India's first World Cup individual gold in men's skeet, a discipline where the country had spent years trying to establish itself internationally, but for Miraj, it wasn't the biggest medal of his career; rather, it was the one that convinced him he still belonged.
"If I didn't win that World Cup, it would be a different Mairaj. That World Cup gold medal gave me another push."
Cairo wasn't an isolated success. Across more than two decades on the international circuit, Mairaj has built one of the most consistent records by an Indian shotgun shooter. His resumr includes three World Cup gold medals - team gold in New Delhi (2021), individual gold in Changwon (2022) and mixed team gold in Cairo (2023) - besides an individual World Cup silver in Rio de Janeiro (2016).
At the Asian Championships, he has won six medals, including team gold in Kuala Lumpur in 2011 and individual silver in Doha in 2019. Commonwealth and South Asian Championship medals followed as Indian shotgun shooting gradually found a place on the international podium.
While the World Cup gold changed how Mairaj looked at himself as an athlete, it has not changed the way he looks at the sport.
One target at a time
"The most important thing in skeet is that it's an outdoor sport. Sometimes it's cold, sometimes it's windy, sometimes it's raining, sometimes there's a tree in the background, sometimes there's a mountain. So visibility keeps changing every time. For you, catching the target is the difficulty."
"Then there is your equipment. Your gun, your stock, ammunition, what kind of spectacles you are wearing, are they enhancing the light? All these things are like pillars of shooting."
There isn't one correct way to shoot. "There are many coaches in the world. They teach different techniques. You can break a target with three-four techniques. But for me, that technique is the easiest. With that, you are breaking the target easily."
Winning, he says, is usually decided somewhere between the body and the mind. "It's a combination of mental and physical. Some shooters are mentally very strong but physically not very fit. Some are physically very fit but don't have a winning mentality. I think it's a balance."
And for Mairaj, pressure never disappears. "Nervousness is a part of being human. You will feel pressure. But how to handle it at that time- that's experience."
"Vincent Hancock also misses targets. But the difference between a loser and a winner is that the winner misses fewer targets. The loser misses more targets. Both miss the targets."
"If you miss one or two targets, don't underestimate yourself. Maybe you miss in the first round. But the next four rounds, you shoot 100 and you make 123. You are in the final. So, never give up. In my diary, there is no word like this. Never give up. 
I'm 50 years old and still working the same. I didn't give up. I don't have the feeling of giving up."
And that process continues as another major championship approaches for Mairaj. "It's a simple logic. One target at a time. You have five rounds. Round by round. After five rounds, we will see the result. If it's in the final, we will run the final. If not, we will sit outside and see."
In a few hours, Mairaj Ahmad Khan will return to the skeet range for his fourth Asian Games, but beyond Nagoya, the pursuit remains the same: an Olympic gold that has occupied his thoughts for more than two decades.
"We have one Olympic champion in shooting. Abhinav Bindra. What's wrong if there are two?"

briefs.headline: ICE officer shoots, wounds man in Austin; protesters demand probe
briefs.bodyText:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday during a brief foot pursuit, local officials said, as the incident drew protests and calls for an independent investigation.
The man, identified by immigration attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch as 28-year-old Venezuelan Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was shot once in the torso and remained in serious but stable condition at a hospital, officials said.
Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the shooting happened after a traffic stop in northern Austin. She cautioned that information about the incident was still preliminary. Austin police were not involved in the shooting, although local investigators were at the scene.
Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry and extremely disappointed” that a person had been shot by ICE in Austin, adding that the city had seen a “significant increase, almost overnight” in ICE operations.
Watson said he wanted Austin police and other local authorities involved in the investigation rather than leaving it solely to ICE.
“I will say, frankly, from my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate,” Watson said.
US Rep Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, had called for an independent investigation shortly after the shooting was reported. He later sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security seeking an immediate, independent probe, the release of all footage from the shooting and accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent involved.
“The horror has come to our city: ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning,” Casar wrote on X, adding that he wanted “truth, transparency and accountability.”
The Travis County district attorney's office also asked for local police and prosecutors to participate in the investigation and requested access to evidence held by federal authorities.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately provide details about the shooting.
Goldfinch said she believed Garces Perez had no criminal history or final order of removal, although she later said she did not know his current immigration status.
The attorney said Garces Perez's family initially struggled to obtain information from the hospital. His wife was later informed that he had been released into ICE custody several hours after the shooting. It was not immediately clear whether he remained at the hospital or had been transferred elsewhere.
About 100 protesters gathered near the shooting site as a large law enforcement presence remained in the area. A dark blue Toyota Corolla with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes was later towed away.
The Austin incident follows other shootings involving immigration agents. In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston after federal agents pursued him in unmarked vehicles.
Another ICE officer shot 25-year-old Colombian man Johan Sebastián in Maine in July. The administration's immigration crackdown has also faced widespread criticism following the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

briefs.headline: Getting away from gunshots
briefs.deck: For many young Israelis, Dharamkot in Himachal Pradesh offers an escape from the pressures of military service and conflict, drawing them to India’s Hummus Trail, in search of peace and healing. Though there has been a marginal dip in visitors after the war, locals in the tranquil Himalayan retreat worry about over tourism, drug use, and rave culture, finds Vikas Vasudeva
briefs.bodyText:
It has been over a week since Jish (name changed to protect privacy) arrived in India after completing his mandatory military service in Israel. He savours a lemon pie and ginger tea at a popular vegan bakery-cum-café located in the narrow market lane of Dharamkot, a misty village in Himachal Pradesh’s rain-washed pine forests. A popular destination among Israeli backpackers along the Hummus Trail, Dharamkot is about two-three kilometres uphill from Mcleodganj. “This is my second visit to India,” he says, just before setting off for his painting class — one of the ways he chooses to unwind in the Himalayan landscape.
He felt compelled to visit last year in May, hearing stories through the drumbeat of social media and his friends’ first-hand accounts. He stayed in the country for nearly five months, first alone, and then for two and half months with his wife. “I travelled mostly in the Himalayas on a motorcycle. I came to Dharamkot, then went to Manali’s Parvati Valley, and then to Ladakh. On my second visit to India, we [my wife and I] have come together,” says Jish, who has served his conscription term of two years in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)’s reserve military service.
Even as the former soldier made plans to travel, the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran left its mark on his life. “Since October 2023, we have lost many friends and many civilians. It’s like an endless war between two nations, the Jewish nation and the Arab nation. Just one month before Hamas attacked us in October 2023, I got engaged. I was on the battlefield. My fiancé prepared all the stuff, you know, the wedding dress, and so on. It’s difficult,” says 25-year-old Jish, who says he joined the IDF when he was 19.
Dharamkot is known as Mini Israel, because a number of Israelis flock here after they complete their conscription terms. Around 80,000 Israelis visit India annually, according to a paper, ‘Decoding the hummus trail of India: regaining the lost prudence’, published in 2022 in Anatolia, an international journal of tourism and hospitality research. “Last year, a little over 1 lakh foreign tourists visited Himachal. This included visitors from Europe, Canada, the U.S., and Israel among other countries,” says Bhanu Gupta, joint director at Himachal’s Tourism department.
This year, however, Dharamkot’s narrow, stone-paved roads lined by tall pine trees look relatively deserted. The influx of Israeli travellers has been skewed and uneven, according to local hospitality players. Yet, over the years, the steady footfall of foreign tourists has helped the economy of this tiny village, even as the locals worry about the adverse impact of drug-laced raves in the forest.
Trailing peace
Jish says he and his wife are “here to relax” and will soon head out on their hired bike to Delhi and onward to Rajasthan. In Dharamkot, “There are different courses, like music sessions, yoga, drawing, and painting — there are so many options to unwind. In India, unlike Israel, there is more peace and Nature, landscapes, and special people,” he says, as he grabs his belongings to move for his painting class in lower Dharamkot, run by residents largely through hired instructors. Charcoal painting and pencil sketching are popular among foreign tourists in this Himalayan village.
For Jish, the trip to India is more than just about travelling. “There is a strong and deep connection between Israel and India, like a religious connection and some shared values between these two nations. India is different from Western societies that are materialistic. The trust factor is what’s really attractive in India,” says Jish, who will soon start a course in Judaism philosophy in Israel this October. He will be in India until then.
The Hummus Trail gets its name from hummus — a Middle Eastern food traditionally made from cooked chickpeas, tahini (sesame paste), lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil. The trail has many cafés and restaurants catering to Israeli travellers. The route spans several places in the mighty mountains of the Himalayas, like Kasol, Old Manali, Rishikesh, and Ladakh. It stretches across Uttar Pradesh’s Varanasi and Pushkar in Rajasthan, extending to South Goa, Gokarna and Hampi in Karnataka, and Vattakanal in Tamil Nadu.
Hodaya, 23, also from Israel, has come to Dharamkot with her friend, drawn by the popularity of the Hummus Trail. “Most Israelis follow the Shvil Hummus (Hummus Trail) route in India and Nepal, as it has many cafés with Hebrew menus, Israeli music, and food. I have been in India for about two months now, travelling between Manali, Leh, and Dharamkot. It’s relaxing here,” says Hodaya, who is set to return to Israel in a couple of days. Asked how she feels about the ongoing conflict, she shrugs it off with a smile, saying, “I am used to it, so I am not stressed anymore.”
Monetising Israeli tourism
The stone walls across Dharamkot are dotted with posters in Hebrew, alongside English. In lower Dharamkot, more accessible by road than the upper areas, the bulletin boards outside cafés, restaurants, roadside stalls, and homestays on the market stretch, serve as a news feed for different events for the village’s international community. There are wellness workshops, music and art events, community activities, and notices for parties.
Narender Pathania, 54, who runs an eight-room guest house in Dharamkot, points out that the flow of Israeli travellers has been unsteady for the past three years. The first lull, he says, was in 2023. That year, on October 7, Hamas-led Palestinian armed groups crossed into southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people.
Soon, the century-old Israel-Palestine conflict — one of the longest and most-violent in the world — escalated, as Israel intensified attacks on Palestine. At least 20,179 children were killed and 44,143 children injured as a direct result of attacks on Gaza between October 7, 2023, and October 7, 2025, according to a UN commission report released on June 23, 2026. “The current total is certainly higher. Thousands of children are feared to be buried under rubble. In the 300 days after the ceasefire was announced 300 more children were killed — one child every day with still hundreds more, injured,” according to UNICEF.
The tourists, Pathania says, further dropped after the US-Israel and Iran conflict broke out in February 2026. “Almost all of them had left when the war with Iran started. Now some have returned, but the flow is lower. All my rooms, which used to be packed during these days, are vacant. It eventually brings loss. Tourism is the primary livelihood for many in our village,” he says.
Pathania adds that Israelis’ Indian sojourn lasts several months, so they prefer budget-friendly homestays over expensive hotels. “Of late, tourists come with their children. Many cafés here cater specifically to the food preferences of Israelis. They visit Manali, Srinagar, Ladakh, and even trek to Chamba from here. They go to meditation centres, lean towards spirituality. Many lie in the lush green field for hours, just relaxing,” he adds.
Vivek Kumar hails from neighbouring Dharamshala, manages routine affairs at ’Dharamkot studio’ that offers pottery and ceramic courses in Dharamkot. He says, “Among the foreigners who come to us, Israelis make up the largest share. We have different courses ranging from five to 35 days. A minimum two-hour workshop is also available to experience the process of shaping wet clay into finished objects. Most of those who enrol with us are Israelis. In their country, these things are quite expensive, as I understand from speaking with them,” he says.
Sanjeev Gandhi, chief advisor to the Hotel and Restaurant Association, Smart City, Dharamshala, who himself runs Hotel Gandhi’s Paradise at Dharamkot, shares his experience on why Israelis are drawn to the town: “Most Israelis come carrying the weight of war and stress. They come to forget. What they value most about Dharamshala is the silence,” says Gandhi, recalling a number of them telling him that the biggest draw is that they don’t hear gunshots.
Not all Israelis need to serve conscription though. There are military exemptions for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, who constitute about 13% of the population. This has triggered protests in the past, also leading to some stress among communities.
Rage against the rave
The Hummus Trail, also notorious as the Hashish Trail, is a route taken for readily available cheap drugs, says the Anatolia paper. In June 2026, taking suo motu action, the Himachal Pradesh High Court directed the transfer of three senior officers, including the then Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police of Kullu district, in connection with the alleged nexus between officials and organisers of big-scale rave parties in Kullu district.
The drug issue was addressed in the 2007 Israeli-Canadian documentary Flipping Out, directed by Yoav Shamir. It follows Israeli soldiers after their discharge as they travel to India, exploring drug use and the psychological breakdowns some experience. The film also documents Israeli officials’ response, including a meeting between the then Deputy Prime Minister Eli Yishai and former soldiers.
Om Prakash Sharma, a former Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) officer, who handled several enforcement operations in Himachal, Punjab, and Jammu-Kashmir, while he worked with the NCB’s Chandigarh zone from 2002 to 2007, asserts that cultivation of cannabis and opium in remote areas of Kullu district and Mandi district of Himachal continues unabated.
“The narcotics trade cannot survive unless there’s support from the socio-political and administrative strata. Foreigners have been found involved in the illicit drug trade,” he says, adding that regular Himachali people get involved because of “local poverty” and “easy money”. The modus operandi is simple — they throw money at people. They know that forest lands and even private lands are available for cultivation at a meagre sum, he says. “These people, usually with Nepalese and other labourers, then cultivate and harvest it, after which the networks of foreigners operate its trade. Foreigners have even been marrying local women as a part of their strategy as well.”
During his tenure, Sharma busted many drug deals, including 155 kilograms of charas (hashish) in Chandigarh, smuggled out of Kullu by Israeli, Czech Republic, and Indian (Kullu) nationals, and bound for Amsterdam in 2005. “During our operations, we had recovered the foreign strain of the cannabis seeds from some foreigners’ houses. That was a hybrid seed, which clearly points to the extent of foreign involvement in the illicit drug trade,” says Sharma, who has also served as convener-cum-advisor of the Himachal Pradesh Nasha Nivaran Board, formed to curb the drug menace.
“Rave parties in secluded forest areas are being organised in the name of tourism, which is not possible without the shelter of bigwigs and administrative machinery and local political patronage,” he adds.
Monika Pathania, former councillor of Dharamkot ward, which falls under Dharamshala Municipal Corporation, says, “People talk about rave parties happening here, but that’s simply not true. Such things don’t happen at all in the village. It could be happening in remote areas where police presence is minimal, but in Dharamkot and neighbouring Bhagsunag there are police check posts to keep a tab on unlawful activities.” She insists the village is only known for its meditation centres.
Ashwani Bamba, president of the Dharamsala Hotel and Restaurant Association, explains that Israelis tend to travel in groups and usually they prefer to spend less on accommodation, but are willing to indulge when it comes to food and, as he puts it, “Other things.” Recalling that things were different a decade or so ago, Bamba points out that then, drug consumption was open. Now, not so much.
Gandhi is worried that locals too are impacted by drugs. “We have been urging the locals and administration to create a joint team to tackle the drug menace,” he says.
For many young Israelis like Jish, Dharamkot is an escape from war, a holiday of healing and hash.

briefs.headline: Heavy rains, squally wind likely in West Bengal from September 22
briefs.deck: A low-pressure area over the east-central Bay of Bengal and adjoining north Andaman Sea is likely to intensify into a depression on Monday, bringing a spell of heavy rain and squally weather to West Bengal from September 22 to September 26
briefs.bodyText:
Parts of West Bengal are likely to receive heavy rainfall with gusty winds from September 22, 2026, due to a deep depression system forming over the Bay of Bengal.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), a low-pressure area over the east-central Bay of Bengal and adjoining north Andaman Sea is likely to intensify into a depression on Monday (September 21, 2026), bringing a spell of heavy rain and squally weather to West Bengal from September 22 to 26.
The intensity of rainfall in Bengal is likely to be higher in the coastal districts of Purba Medinipur and South 24 Parganas, with gusty winds reaching speeds of 40-50 kmph, it said.
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds, reaching speeds of 30-40 kmph, are likely in one or two places in the remaining districts of south Bengal, including Kolkata, till September 25, the weather office said.
It said heavy rainfall will also occur in the sub-Himalayan districts of Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Jalpaiguri, Alipurduar and Cooch Behar from September 23 to 25.
Thunderstorms with gusty winds are likely over the other north Bengal districts of Uttar and Dakshin Dinajpur as well as Malda during the period, the IMD added.
"Continuing to move west-northwestwards, it is very likely to reach the west-central and adjoining northwest Bay of Bengal near the north Andhra Pradesh — South Odisha coasts around the morning of 23rd September. Southwest monsoon moderate to strong over Andaman Sea; moderate over Northeast, Eastcentral, Southeast Bay of Bengal; weak to moderate over Northwest, Westcentral, Southwest Bay of Bengal," said IMD.
IMD also advised the fishermen not to venture into the deep sea from 21st September along and off West Bengal coast and from 22nd September to 25th September. Fishermen are advised to return to the coast by the night of 21st September.
"Swell waves in the range of 16.0 - 19.0 sec period with 0.9 - 1.1 m height are forecast up to 20:30 hours on 21-09-2026. It was advised that there is a possibility of surging waves; boats to ply with utmost vigilance; recreation with due care," said IMD in its statement.

stories.headline: Offer ‘tips’ to good officers, says Karnataka minister, lands in soup
stories.bodyText:
HASSAN: Hassan district minister KM Shivalingegowda’s statement that there is “nothing wrong” if citizens happily give ‘tips’ or ‘honorarium’ to govt officials for timely work has triggered outrage among the public and 
BJP
.
The minister made the comment during ‘Prajaseva Andolana’, a public-grievances meet, here Saturday.
Puneeth, a farmer from Alur taluk in the district who was attending the meeting to highlight his land case, condemned the statement in front of the minister. “Officials are paid a salary. Why should we give them tips? Doesn’t this amount to encouraging bribery?” Puneeth and a group of youths questioned the minister directly. With more people backing them, the meeting witnessed chaos.
Sensing the situation going out of hand, Shivalingegowda tried to defend himself. “I meant officials should not extort money. I said honest workers should be respected, not that bribery should be encouraged,” he said.
The minister Sunday clarified: “A person complained that bribe was being sought to get his work done. I told him not to give any money, but to respect the officer. 
My statement has been misunderstood,” Gowda said.
Deputy commissioner KS Latha Kumari pacified the protesters. “The minister’s statement has been misinterpreted. If officials demand bribes for work, stringent legal action will be taken against them,” she said.
BJP MLC 
CT Ravi
, on his ‘X’ account, condemned the minister for his remarks. Ravi has mentioned that chief minister 
D K Shivakumar
 had said that if anyone asks for even Rs 10 as a bribe, complain to him. But ministers of his own govt are saying ‘respectfully give bribes’. “It may be natural for you to receive or give bribes, minister, but not for the people of Karnataka.”
The MLC urged the minister to withdraw the statement and say sorry to the people of the state.

stories.headline: Volunteers plog and plant, lead awareness on World Cleanup Day weekend in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The second day of World Cleanup Day weekend saw students and citizens turn out in large numbers for activities as part of the Times of India’s #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks, presented by Multigen and in association with Kristu Jayanti University.
At BDA Doddakallasandra Parks 1 and 2, Youth for Seva led a mega plogging and clean-up drive, with students from RV University and City Engineering College joining in large numbers. This was followed by Kempabudhi Lake Park, where volunteers participated in a vegetable seed plantation activity led by Adamya Chetana. At Yediyur Lake Park, students from Christ University, Central Campus, turned up for a plogging and waste segregation awareness activity led by Indian Ploggers Army.
Highlighting the need to translate climate awareness into action, Plog Raja, Indian Ploggers Army, said, “World Cleanup Day reminds us that climate action cannot stop at awareness; it has to move to the ground. Through initiatives like #IamBengaluru, we are seeing that action take shape in our own neighbourhoods, with citizens, and increasingly Gen Z, showing up to care for the public spaces.”
For Youth for Seva, volunteering is also about building a deeper culture of civic responsibility. 
Raghavendra BS, volunteer management head - Karnataka, YFS, said, “Volunteering is rooted in the idea that what we receive from society and nature creates a responsibility to give back. #IamBengaluru turns that belief into everyday civic action. When citizens clean a park, manage waste responsibly or nurture its greenery, they are not just improving a public space, but expressing gratitude to the community and environment that sustain us. Our aspiration is to build a culture where such service becomes a natural part of being a responsible citizen.” To participate in future volunteering events, register at https://iambengaluru.co.in.
Spoorti Joshi, first-year student, RV University, said, “We collected over 80kg of waste from just one park, which showed me how much a few hours of collective effort can achieve. Volunteering is also about creating awareness that the waste we throw away can affect birds, animals and the larger ecosystem.”
Sushruth, NSS volunteer, RV University added Bengaluru may be an IT city, but people also need green spaces where they can step away from work and breathe. “Keeping these parks clean is our responsibility as citizens, and even a little of our time can help.”
Annika Chourasia, RV University, said, “In the hustle of Bengaluru, we often forget to spend time with nature and contribute to the city around us. Spending a Sunday volunteering with friends genuinely made my day. If each of us can give even an hour a week to something we care about, it can add up to a meaningful change.”
Mamatha, JP Nagar 8th Phase resident, said this was her fifth #IamBengaluru volunteering activity. “My mother always told me that what matters is not what you get from society, but what you give back to it. Even one hour of volunteering gives me a sense of fulfilment,” she said.
Rakshitha, Jayanagar resident, said, “A park is one of the few places where you see people of every age spending time together, with family, friends and nature. In a city where fresh air and greenery are increasingly precious, keeping these shared spaces clean matters to everyone who uses them.”
Veena Kaulgud, Kengeri resident, added, “Growing up with Bengaluru’s identity as the Garden City made its greenery special to me. Tree planting has now become a weekly activity, and every plantation drive by 
TOI and Adamya Chetana is close to my heart. As a regular 
TOI
 reader, I was especially happy to see #IamBengaluru bring more people into caring for the city’s parks.”

stories.headline: FSDA cancels 16 pharmacy licences, suspends 8, including Pfizer depot
stories.deck: The action follows the department’s investigation into a large-scale unlicenced drug repacking and relabelling racket uncovered at a farmhouse in Bengaluru South district’s Bidadi on August 18.
stories.bodyText:
The Karnataka Food Safety and Drugs Administration (FSDA) has cancelled the licences of 16 pharmaceutical retailers and wholesalers and suspended those of eight others, including the licence of multinational firm Pfizer’s depot in Nelamangala, in connection with the ongoing investigation into the alleged distribution and sale of spurious drugs.
The action follows the department’s investigation into a large-scale unlicenced drug repacking and relabelling racket uncovered at a farmhouse in Bengaluru South district’s Bidadi on August 18. The FSDA had seized spurious drugs, machinery and printing material worth ₹5.05 crore from the premises. When the preliminary investigation revealed the potential involvement of a large network, the State government formed a Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by IPS officer C. Vamsi Krishna.
Health Minister U.T. Khader addressed the press on Sunday (September 20) and said the licences of suspicious firms/pharmacies had been cancelled and those of a few others suspended for not cooperating with the SIT’s investigation. “We have stopped Pfizer’s sale in the State because they did not cooperate with the investigation,” Mr. Khader said. He added that he could not reveal much about the case as the SIT was investigating.
The Minister further stressed that strict action would be taken against those named in the SIT report after the investigation, regardless of how powerful or influential they might be.
When questioned about where people should go for medicines in such a situation, Mr. Khader said, “At present, everything is original in the government hospitals,” reiterating that medicines at government hospitals are safe.
Licences cancelled and suspended
According to the list shared by the FSDA, the firms whose licences have been cancelled include Avesco Healthcare in Prabhakar Reddy Layout, Bengaluru Speciality Pharma in Shivajinagar, Museum Road in Chamarajpet; Patel Medi Trade in Jayanagar, N.S. Pharma in Hubballi, and Sagar Pharma in Kumaraswamy Layout, among others.
The firms whose licences have been suspended include Sagar Pharma in Tilak Nagar, Surya Speciality Hospital in Bommasandra Industrial Area, and Vivanta Pharmaceuticals in Jayanagar, among others.
In a press statement, the FSDA urged citizens to buy medicines from licenced pharmacies and against valid tax invoices. It also urged people to report suspicious packaging or non-functional QR codes on drug labels.
What is the case?
According to the FSDA, the accused allegedly procured low-cost medicines from neighbouring States, refilled them into new vials and relabelled them as expensive, life-saving drugs of multinational companies. The department also seized 30 boxes of expired drugs, along with injection-filling machinery, forged labels and stamps.
The FSDA said the batch numbers and entries of the seized drugs had been blocked on its portal to prevent their further sale or distribution. Samples have also been sent for laboratory testing to verify their chemical composition, sterility and potency.
The department noted that the premises in Bidadi were being used to manufacture, store and distribute drugs without a valid licence. A criminal case has been registered under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

stories.headline: Greater Bengaluru Authority faces backlash over ‘software charge’ on property owners
stories.deck: The five city corporations under the GBA have started collecting the ₹200 charge from property owners along with the annual property tax.
stories.bodyText:
The Greater Bengaluru Authority’s (GBA) decision to levy a ₹200 ‘software charge’ from property owners has triggered criticism from citizens, who have questioned the need for yet another levy when they are already paying property tax and garbage cess.
The five city corporations under the GBA have started collecting the ₹200 charge from property owners along with the annual property tax. For commercial properties, officials said the charge would be ₹1,000. There has been no official announcement from the GBA explaining the levy. Officials, however, said the annual charge was being collected towards the “maintenance” of digital services and software.
Property owners have questioned why citizens should be made to pay separately for software and digital services, particularly when several basic civic services remain inadequate. They have questioned why they are being asked to pay a separate annual charge for software and digital services that civic bodies were already using.
“If this is being added as a separate charge, citizens deserve a clear explanation of what it covers, the legal basis for it and where that money goes. We take pride in calling Bengaluru an IT city, but why should we pay ₹200 for the GBA to run its IT services?” said Veda Murthy, a property owner in Kodigehalli.
Others questioned the levy in the context of the city’s existing civic problems. “From roads to streetlights, garbage collection, garbage tax and the helpline system, nothing has improved. But citizens are just being looted every day in the name of some or the other tax,” said Nataraj B.
Several citizens have also taken to social media to oppose the charge, demanding transparency on its purpose and utilisation and calling for it to be withdrawn.
The move has also drawn criticism from political parties.
Srikanth Narasimhan, founder and general secretary of the Bengaluru NavaNirmana Party (BNP), linked the levy to the absence of elected local representatives in Bengaluru, saying that decisions imposing financial burdens on citizens were being taken without adequate public scrutiny. “Before imposing another levy, GBA must disclose the accounts, justify the charges and be held accountable to the people,” he said.
BJP State president B.Y. Vijayendra also criticised the levy, calling it the latest “innovation” of the Congress government’s governance in Karnataka. “What exactly are citizens paying for? Why should people separately fund the government’s software system? Where is the legal basis, cost breakup and public accountability?” he questioned.

briefs.headline: After traffic outrage, minister reviews road works in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Amid outrage over schoolchildren spending hours in traffic and worsening congestion on the Varthur-Gunjur stretch (SH-35), Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda convened a high-level review meeting and directed officials to prioritise pothole repairs, warning that contractors could face action if delays persist.
The meeting was attended by officials from Karnataka Road Development Corporation Ltd (KRDCL), Bescom, Bengaluru East City Corporation (BECC), GBA, the additional chief secretary (ACS) and other senior officials involved in infrastructure works.
Gowda directed contractors to immediately repair potholes and damaged stretches between Brigade developments and Gunjur, while prioritising repairs on Varthur-Kodi Road. Sources said officials, when questioned about delays, pointed to the contractor, while also acknowledging difficulties related to land acquisition.
Bescom officials, including its managing director, were questioned over delays in shifting electric poles and power infrastructure—an issue residents and officials have repeatedly cited as a major factor slowing road works along the corridor.
The intervention comes days after residents highlighted severe congestion on SH-35, with some schoolchildren reportedly taking more than two hours to travel a few kilometres in school buses, triggering widespread public outrage.
Officials said the ACS has called both contractors for a meeting Monday to explain the delays. “If there’s no concrete explanation, the ACS is likely to recommend replacing the contractors,” a source familiar with the discussions told TOI.
Meanwhile, there were signs of movement on the ground. Local representatives told TOI that contractor representatives visited parts of the Varthur-Gunjur stretch Sunday to assess pending works, while the KRDCL chief engineer also inspected the site.
Residents said that if the contractor is deliberately delaying the project or failing to work, the agency should be replaced immediately. They added that the minister and authorities must now shift focus from meetings and inspections to visible progress on the ground.

briefs.headline: Pocso accused PE teacher dies by suicide at SP office in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: A 49-year-old physical education teacher, who was accused in a Pocso case, allegedly jumped from the third floor of the Bengaluru South district superintendent of police (SP) office Sunday afternoon.
The deceased is Shashidhar from , a native of Vijayanagar. He had been working at an aided high school in Channapatna taluk for the past 15 years.
A Pocso case had been registered against Shashidhar following allegations of sexual abuse of five minor girls studying in the school. An FIR was registered at Ramanagara women’s police station Saturday, while police had arrested him the same evening.
Police on Sunday morning brought him to the Measurement Collection Unit (MCU), located in the Bengaluru South district SP office, after a medical examination to register his fingerprints.
Jumps From Third Floor
After completion of the procedures, police were taking him downstairs from the third floor when he suddenly jumped from the building around 12 pm. He was rushed to a nearby hospital, but doctors declared him brought dead.
Shashidhar’s family members alleged that baseless allegations had been levelled against him and alleged that he had been subjected to severe mental pressure by the police and school management, which drove him to take the extreme step.

briefs.headline: 46-year-old man found dead inside luxury car parked on Koramangala road in Bengaluru
briefs.deck: A 46-year-old man was found dead in a high-end vehicle on Sunday morning. Identified as Salim Akbar from Kodagu, he was discovered unresponsive. Initial investigations and security camera footage revealed the car had been parked near a restaurant around 2:30 am. While authorities are awaiting further reports, they suspect health issues may have played a role in the death, with no indications of…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A 46-year-old man was found dead inside a luxury car parked on a main road in Koramangala on Sunday morning, police said.
The deceased was identified as Salim Akbar, a native of Kodagu.
Police received information around 8 am about a luxury car parked on the road with a man inside. A police team reached the spot and found Akbar unresponsive.
He was taken to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared him dead. His body has been shifted for an autopsy.
According to preliminary investigation and CCTV footage, the car had pulled over in front of a restaurant in the area around 2.30 am, police said. They suspect that he may have died due to health issues.
However, the exact cause of death will be established after the forensic and autopsy reports, police said. No foul play is suspected at this stage, they added.
Scene-of-crime officers and forensic investigators examined the car.
Police registered an unnatural death report.
(With Agency Inputs)

briefs.headline: ‘Hands off our lakes’: Citizens oppose Bengaluru’s Hebbal short tunnel
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A group of citizens gathered at Hebbal Lake Sunday opposing the use of lake land and its buffer for the Rs 1,140-crore short tunnel project, warning that construction in the already flood-prone area could worsen waterlogging and damage the lake’s ecological health.
Holding banners that read ‘Leave Our Lakes Alone’ and ‘Kere Beku, Tunnel Beda’ (We want lakes, not tunnels), the citizens said Bengaluru’s waterbodies and tree cover could not be sacrificed for infrastructure projects. The protesters also pointed to the long history of Hebbal Lake, one of Bengaluru’s major waterbodies, and said years of sewage inflow, encroachment and unplanned infrastructure had already degraded the lake.
Rohini, a protester, said, “Pouring concrete over lakes and reservoirs is as suicidal as willfully blocking one’s own arteries.”
Rahul, a resident, said the project went against the legacy associated with 
Kempegowda
, whose statue stands opposite the lake. “I remember reading that his mother told him, ‘Keregalum Kattu, Marangalum Nedu’, which translates to ‘Build many lakes and plant many trees’. But how are we following this legacy? The lake is being used for the short tunnel and more than 1,000 trees will be removed,” he said.
The 2.2-km short tunnel is among the infrastructure projects being scrutinised over its impact on the lake. Earlier, Karnataka high court had sought details on whether the project would affect Hebbal Lake’s inflow and outflow as well as underground water flow.
An IISc study cited during the proceedings had also raised concerns over the project, including the possibility of congestion shifting to other points and issues related to the tunnel’s entry and exit locations and the existing flyover infrastructure.

briefs.headline: Karnataka SIR: Deletions in Bengaluru disproportionately high, 12 seats cross 10-times winning margin mark
briefs.deck: Bommanahalli Assembly constituency has recorded the highest deletions during the draft stage; constituencies with high deletions are also seeing a large number of notices being issued
briefs.bodyText:
At least 12 of Bengaluru’s 28 Assembly constituencies have seen the number of voters deleted from the draft electoral roll exceed 10 times the winning margin in the 2023 Assembly election. The pattern of deletions points to a large number of names – more than 90% in some constituencies – being marked as either shifted or absent.
For instance, in Bommanahalli Assembly constituency, which has recorded the highest deletions during the draft stage (54%), the winning margin in 2023 was 24,215 votes, while more than 2.65 lakh names have been deleted under the Absent, Shifted, Duplicate, Dead and Others (ASDDO) category — nearly 11 times the winning margin.
In Dasarahalli, where the winning margin was 9,194 votes, the number of deletions is more than 26 times the margin. The constituency has seen more than 2.45 lakh deletions, the second-highest at 52% of the electorate.
The constituencies with high deletions are also seeing a large number of notices being issued. There are also instances of what appear to be mass deletions, with an overwhelming number of voters marked as shifted and large numbers of deletions concentrated in the same polling stations.
For instance, in C.V. Raman Nagar, over 1.40 lakh names have been deleted – 8.5 times the winning margin of 16,395 votes. Of the remaining 1.33 lakh electors, 60% have been marked for notices, with more than 80,840 receiving notices.
Moreover, across Bommanahalli, Dasarahalli and C.V. Raman Nagar, an overwhelming share of the deletions is in the shifted and absent categories.
In Bommanahalli, shifted and absent together account for 95% of the deletions, with 50.34% marked as shifted and 45.38% as absent. Similarly, in Dasarahalli, over 73% are marked as shifted and 20.54% as absent, together accounting for 93% of the deletions. The trend is similar in C.V. Raman Nagar, where the two categories together account for 92% of the deletions.
Data suggest that the 28 Assembly constituencies in Bengaluru have been disproportionately affected by the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. While Bengaluru account for less than one-fifth of Karnataka’s electors, the deletion rate here is 45%, compared to 13.5% in the rest of the State, while the rate of notices is more than eight times higher.
Mass deletions
The booth-level data compiled by Mandate Analytics and Consulting (MAC) Insights, an independent electoral intelligence and data consultancy, also suggests instances of mass deletions.
In BBMP North, Part 301 recorded a deletion rate of over 93% – of the 1,129 electors in the 2025 data, 1,053 have been deleted. The Part 53 in Malleswaram and Part 311 in K.R. Pura recorded deletion rates of 85% and 83%, respectively. Within Bengaluru Urban, at least six booths, all in the Bengaluru South constituency, have recorded deletions of more than 80%.

briefs.headline: OFC menace persists in Bengaluru as new GBA regulations remain pending
briefs.deck: Even busy stretches in the city, such as Hosur Road, Mysore Road, Indiranagar 100 Feet Road, Brigade Road, Bannerghatta Road and Koramangala 80 Feet Road (Ganesh Temple), have cables hanging low, bunched to trees, snapped and lying on footpaths and roads.
briefs.bodyText:
The dangling and low-hanging Optical Fibre Cables (OFCs) continue to pose a threat to pedestrians and motorists in Bengaluru, even as fresh bylaws to tighten regulations governing the use of roads for OFCs await discussion at the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).
A reality check by The Hindu shows that even busy stretches in the city, such as Hosur Road, Mysore Road, Indiranagar 100 Feet Road, Brigade Road, Bannerghatta Road and Koramangala 80 Feet Road (Ganesh Temple), have cables hanging low, bunched to trees, snapped and lying on footpaths and roads.
For instance, JNC Road in Koramangala is one of the busiest stretches on all days and sees an increased crowd on weekends. A private college located on the stretch makes it crucial, with hundreds of students using it every day. In addition, several restaurants located on the adjoining street bring thousands of people to the locality.
Aarti, a student of the private college, said that snapped OFCs are a common sight on the stretch, and such a situation, compounded by haphazard parking along the stretch, makes it impossible for pedestrians to walk, especially during rush hours.
“There is a severe parking issue on this stretch, which hasn’t been addressed. Hundreds of students walk to the bus stop near Hosur Road, and the entire way of about 600 metres is flooded with such cables,” she said.
Connectivity woes
Pravar Choudhary, an architect, pointed out that stretches with wider footpaths, such as Indiranagar 100 Feet Road, are also covered with bunched cables, creating safety issues. “More people will start accessing footpaths if obstructions like OFCs are eliminated,” he said.
Several daily commuters who access public transport said such obstructions affect first and last-mile connectivity, leading to increased vehicles on roads and congestion. Despite being a perennial issue that adds to the flawed pedestrian infrastructure, the civic body has failed to strictly enforce rules and curb illegal OFC connections.
Previous enforcement
According to data from the erstwhile Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP), between 2012 and 2025, aggregators established over 15,000 km of OFC lines within the city limits. Since 2023, OFC permissions were put on hold until mid-2025. However, 150 km of OFC lines were illegally created by aggregators.
Meanwhile, data also shows that the civic body imposed fines in only 118 instances for violating OFC rules between 2017 and 2022. A senior GBA official said that since permissions were temporarily put on hold, the civic body hasn’t imposed fines thereafter. However, according to other sources, there wasn’t much vigil, and illegal connections had been established despite a blanket ban.
A city corporation commissioner told The Hindu that the OFC subject is still centralised and managed at the GBA level, leaving little scope for corporations to fully enforce the rules. “To disconnect and remove illegal connections, ground-level data is unavailable. Without granular information, we cannot clear illegal OFC lines,” he said, stressing that it will disrupt the internet services.
Another officer said that many telecom aggregators are shifting to underground ducts, but there is also a court case related to the shifting, and once that is cleared, enforcing the underground OFC mandate will be relatively easy. “Many aggregators were not on board with paying separate fees for moving to underground ducts, and this escalated,” he said.
The GBA officer explained that to address the OFC issues, bylaws were drafted earlier this year, tightening regulations by specifying the requirements for laying cables, the structures that can be used and the length of cables. “The bylaws draft was proposed twice, but there is no movement yet. It has to be discussed in the executive committee meeting, but the topic hasn’t come up yet,” the officer said.
Continues to haunt people
The OFC menace continues to be unresolved even as the city corporations have taken up footpath clearance drives.
Dhruv N.K., a civic activist from South Bengaluru, said pedestrian infrastructure is a complex issue with multiple factors, with OFCs being a major issue. “GBA’s initiative to improve pedestrian infrastructure is limited to clearing street vendors and fails to cover more contributing aspects such as OFC, broken footpaths, and drains uncovered with slabs. Acting on easy targets and not addressing other issues defeats the purpose,” he said.
Clement Jayakumar of Mahadevapura Task Force added that the GBA should at least focus on clearing cables hanging lower than 10 metres. “There is also a design issue when it comes to connecting multiple lines. With the bylaws, there is a need for redrawing the design for establishing multiple connections from one common point,” he said, adding that it will address the low-hanging wires issue as well.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru Traffic Police books record 10.99 lakh wrong parking cases, yet menace continues to haunt Bengaluru
briefs.deck: The problem persists even as towing, paid parking, and dedicated beats have been initiated to address the issue
briefs.bodyText:
A whopping 10.99 lakh wrong parking cases have been booked by the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP) in the first eight months of this year, nearly matching the 11.16 lakh cases booked in the whole of last year, which itself was a record.
While the data suggests that enforcement has tightened, the officers admitted that there has been very little impact on the ground. The problem persists even as towing, paid parking, and dedicated beats have been initiated to address the issue.
A senior traffic police officer blamed the low penalty and recurring concession offers floated by the government for hindering the impact of tighter enforcement. As a result, haphazard parking still thrives in the city, although it is one of the major contributors to micro-level congestion, which also impacts traffic on arterial roads.
Record enforcement, persistent problem
According to data accessed by The Hindu, this is the highest number of cases booked in the corresponding period in any of the last 10 years, for wrong parking. Further, the data shows that the BTP booked 11.16 lakh wrong parking cases in the whole of 2025, 9.73 lakh in 2024, 10 lakh each in 2023 and 2022, and 7.26 lakh in 2021.
In addition, the BTP has booked a record 1.16 lakh footpath parking cases till end of August, 2026, while no year in the last half a decade saw more than 90,000 cases booked in the first eight months.
The officers noted that it is natural for a city like Bengaluru, with an increasing number of vehicle registrations, to record increased violations and a year-on-year increase in the number of cases.
Low fines?
A senior traffic police officer explained that Bengaluru has lower fines for haphazard parking, at ₹500, compared with other cities. He opined that it should be over ₹1,000 for a first-time violation, with the fines increasing through fixed slabs for second and third-time violations.
“In addition, we keep giving concessions for violators, which defeats the purpose of penalising. There are many instances where motorists who are caught violating norms, leave by saying they will pay the fines when the traffic police roll out the concession window,” the officer explained.
The lower fine structure was also recently flagged by Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda, who had even written to the Transport Minister, urging an increase in the penalty for driving on footpaths. The haphazard parking also falls in the same category.
